chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Behavioral Economics Is (and Isn't)

lessons.title: Behavioral Economics vs Behavioral Finance: Why This Isn't a Repeat

children.text: Ritika manages a ₹40 crore book of retail clients at a broking firm in Mumbai. She spots loss aversion the moment a client refuses to sell a stock trading 30% below cost, and she has seen enough IPO frenzies to recognise herd mentality from a distance. Then she goes home, buys a ₹65,000 phone on a "No Cost EMI" plan without checking the flat interest rate hidden inside it, keeps paying for three subscriptions she forgot she had because cancelling felt like a hassle, and still hasn't bought the health insurance policy she has been meaning to buy for two years. The same brain that reads a client's portfolio clearly is making all these other decisions badly, and it isn't because Ritika lacks financial literacy. Loss aversion, present bias and plain inertia don't stay inside a demat account. They run through every economic decision a person makes. This lesson draws the line between the behavioral finance you may already know and the wider field this course is built on.

body.text: Behavioral economics is the parent field. It studies how real, imperfectly rational people make any economic decision: spending, saving, insuring, negotiating, voting on policy. Behavioral finance is one branch of it, applied specifically to investing and financial markets. Knowing the branch doesn't mean you know the tree.

children.text: Behavioral Finance Is a Branch, Not the Whole Field

markDefs.definition: A theoretical figure economists use in classical models: a person who is purely rational, fully informed, and acts only in their own self-interest. Real people are not this, which is precisely what behavioral economics studies.

children.text: If you have gone through investor psychology material before, you already know the core cast: loss aversion, anchoring, overconfidence, the disposition effect, herd behavior. Behavioral finance takes standard finance theory, built on the assumption that investors are rational and markets are efficient, and corrects it using psychology. It asks a narrow question: why do real investors and real markets deviate from what rational-agent models predict?

Behavioral economics asks a much bigger question. It takes standard economics itself, built on the same fictional rational actor, and asks the same thing about every economic decision, not only investing. Why do employees skip a pension scheme even when it is free money from their employer? Why does a ₹499 item marked down from ₹999 sell faster than the same ₹499 item priced plainly? Why do government savings schemes need auto-enrolment to actually get used? Why do banks sometimes fail not because they are insolvent but because everyone believes everyone else will withdraw first? None of these are investing questions, yet all of them are behavioral economics questions.

columns.label: Behavioral finance
points: Applies psychology specifically to investing and financial markets
Explains anomalies like momentum, bubbles, and excess volatility
Reference theory it corrects: the Efficient Market Hypothesis and CAPM
Typical subject: the retail investor, the portfolio manager, the trader
Typical question: why did the Nifty overreact to one disappointing earnings print?

columns.label: Behavioral economics
points: Applies psychology to any economic decision, investing included
Explains anomalies in pricing, saving, insurance, policy, and negotiation
Reference theory it corrects: standard microeconomics and homo economicus
Typical subject: the consumer, the employee, the taxpayer, the regulator
Typical question: why do people underinsure even when the numbers clearly favor buying cover?

children.text: A Short History: From One Paper to Two Nobel Prizes

Both fields trace back to the same handful of psychologists and economists. The timeline below is worth knowing, because it explains why behavioral economics is now standard vocabulary in central banks, regulators, and consulting firms rather than a fringe academic idea.

events.title: Prospect Theory is published
events.description: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky publish "Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk" in Econometrica, showing people weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains. This is the founding paper of behavioral economics.

events.title: Kahneman wins the Nobel
events.description: Daniel Kahneman receives the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for integrating psychological research into economics. Tversky had died in 1996 and the prize is not awarded posthumously.

events.title: Nudge is published
events.description: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein publish "Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness," turning behavioral economics into a practical tool for designing policy and products.

events.title: The world's first government nudge unit
events.description: The UK Cabinet Office sets up the Behavioural Insights Team, quickly nicknamed the "Nudge Unit," to apply behavioral economics directly to public policy.

events.title: Thaler wins the Nobel
events.description: Richard Thaler receives the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to behavioral economics, including mental accounting and nudge design.

events.title: India's Economic Survey adopts the framework
events.description: India's Economic Survey 2018-19 devotes a full chapter, titled "Policy for Homo Sapiens, Not Homo Economicus," to using behavioral nudges in government programmes such as the Swachh Bharat Mission and the Give It Up LPG subsidy campaign.

stats.label: Countries with a government nudge unit
stats.context: Per an OECD review of behavioral insights teams worldwide

body.text: If a concept in this course feels familiar, like loss aversion or anchoring, that is intentional. The same handful of biases resurfaces across every branch of behavioral economics. What changes is the setting: a demat account in behavioral finance, a food-delivery app's checkout page in Chapter 3, and a government subsidy scheme in Chapter 4.

children.text: Why This Matters Beyond Your Portfolio

As a finance professional, your clients, employer, and the regulators you work under are all economic actors making non-investing decisions every day: whether to insure adequately, how to price a product, whether to switch a retirement default, whether to trust a bank enough not to queue outside it. Understanding only the investing slice of behavioral science leaves you blind to the rest of the picture. This course moves outward, one chapter at a time.

body.title: Spot the field
body.question: Which of these is a behavioral finance question rather than a broader behavioral economics question?
options: Why do salaried employees leave free employer pension matching on the table?
Why does a stock's price overreact to one disappointing quarterly result?
Why does "Flat 70% Off" sell better than the same final price shown plainly?
Why do people under-enrol in a health insurance plan even when the expected value clearly favors buying it?
body.explanation: Option B is about how a financial market prices new information, which is squarely behavioral finance territory. The other three involve saving, pricing psychology, and insurance, none of which involve a traded market price at all, which is why they belong to the wider field of behavioral economics.

body.title: Same bias, different field
body.scenario: Rohan is a wealth manager. He has spent years explaining to clients why holding onto a losing stock out of stubbornness, the disposition effect, is a mistake. His own employer offers a better pension fund option with lower fees and a stronger historical return than the default fund Rohan was auto-enrolled into eight years ago. He has never switched, even though the paperwork would take fifteen minutes.
body.prompt: Is Rohan's failure to switch pension funds a behavioral finance problem or a behavioral economics problem, and which bias is most likely driving it? (Hint: it isn't the disposition effect, that one is about selling, not staying put.)
body.modelAnswer:
1. It is a behavioral economics problem rather than a behavioral finance one in the narrow sense. There is no market price move Rohan is reacting to; he is failing to act on a straightforward decision about savings and defaults.
2. The likely driver is status quo bias combined with inertia: the default fund, set eight years ago, has never been actively revisited, and the switching cost feels larger than fifteen minutes because the benefit of switching is invisible day to day.
3. This is exactly the kind of decision behavioral economics studies that narrow behavioral finance, focused on market prices and investor behavior in markets, would not typically cover.
4. The realistic fix mirrors what policy designers use elsewhere in this course: a better default, a reminder, or lower switching friction, not simply repeating the numbers to Rohan again.

body.title: Field versus branch
body.textWithBlank: Behavioral economics is the ___ field; behavioral finance is one branch of it, applied specifically to investing and markets.
body.explanation: Behavioral economics is the umbrella discipline covering any economic decision. Behavioral finance narrows that same psychology down to investing and financial markets specifically.

body.title: Is "homo economicus" a real term economists use?

children.text: Yes, though no economist claims people actually behave this way at every moment. The term dates back to nineteenth-century critiques of classical economics built on Adam Smith and John Stuart Mill's simplifying assumption that economic actors reason purely in their own self-interest with complete information. Homo economicus is a modeling shortcut, useful for building clean, solvable theories, but a poor description of how anyone actually decides whether to buy insurance, switch a pension fund, or negotiate a raise. Behavioral economics exists because that gap between the model and real behavior turned out to be too large and too predictable to ignore.

body.context: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory paper led to Kahneman's 2002 Nobel Prize and, fifteen years later, Thaler's 2017 Nobel Prize for extending the same ideas into policy design and finance.

cards.definition: The study of how real, imperfectly rational people make any economic decision, from spending and saving to insuring, negotiating, and voting on policy.
The branch of behavioral economics applied specifically to investing and financial markets, explaining why investors and markets deviate from rational-agent predictions.
The theoretical, purely rational, self-interested, fully informed decision maker assumed by classical economic models. Not a description of real people.

Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 theory showing people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains. The founding idea of behavioral economics.
A change in how choices are presented that predictably shifts behavior without banning any option or changing the underlying economic incentives. Coined by Thaler and Sunstein in 2008.

points: Behavioral economics is the parent field studying how real people make any economic decision. Behavioral finance is one branch of it, applied to investing and markets specifically.
If you already know biases like loss aversion or anchoring from investing content, you already have the raw material for this course. Only the setting changes.
The field traces to Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory paper, and has since earned two Nobel Prizes and become a standard tool in Indian public policy.
A question with no market price attached, like why people underinsure or don't switch a pension fund, is a behavioral economics question, not a behavioral finance one.
This course moves outward from everyday money decisions to business pricing, government policy, the workplace, and finally the whole economy.
